boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Monroe's Cross Roads record (March 10, 1865) in the Carolinas Campaign [February-March 1865]. The night movements of March 9 near Solemn Grove and the occupation of Fayetteville on March 11 are context outside the record. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads Kilpatrick's Cavalry Division (1,850) against Wheeler's and Hampton's cavalry (3,000); the live field reads 4,900 (US 1,850; CS 3,050). Kilpatrick reports 5,068 men for duty in his command at the start of the campaign, and says he took post with Spencer's small brigade of three regiments, 400 dismounted men and a section of artillery, that less than one-third of his command was attacked, and that the attackers were three divisions (Humes's, Allen's and Butler's), the entire Confederate cavalry under Hampton. Wheeler says he took command of his own and Butler's cavalry for the charge; his synopsis gives his corps' effective force as 4,442 at the start of the campaign, 5,172 in his February 16 reports and 4,965 on April 17.
claims.rationale: Kilpatrick's 5,068 and Wheeler's effective totals are campaign or other-date figures, not counts engaged on March 10; Kilpatrick's 'less than one-third' is a proportion without a base date. The live CS 3,050 differs from the frozen 3,000. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Kilpatrick says he reached the position after a march over horrible roads, swamps and swollen streams and took post where a road intersects the Morgantown road; after the first charge his men were forced back about 500 yards to a swamp impassable to either side, where they rallied. NPS places the two brigades' camps near the Charles Monroe House.
claims.rationale: The roads and swamp predate the action; the choice of camp was made the night before it. The tag stays unresolved.

claims.value: Kilpatrick describes his three brigades at the start of the campaign as indifferently mounted and badly armed. He says the Confederates, eager for plunder, did not promptly follow up and were trying to harness the battery horses and plunder his headquarters when he counterattacked, and that he captured 150 horses with their equipment. Wheeler says his men at one time held the Union artillery and wagons, cut down the wagons and drove off the mules.
claims.rationale: Equipment and capture statements from interested reports; no ordnance, horse or transport return inspected.

claims.value: Kilpatrick says prisoners reported Hampton's cavalry some miles in the rear marching for Fayetteville, scouts reported it on two roads, he posted a brigade on each and took a third road himself, and in the evening rode with his staff through one of Hampton's divisions; Atkins and Jordan found about 9 o'clock that the Confederates were passing their main force by a road to the right and could not reach him before daylight, and his command was attacked unexpectedly. Wheeler says he reconnoitred Kilpatrick's camps with Hampton on the night of the 9th. NPS says Hampton surprised the Federals in their camps.
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from interested reports and a modern summary; the scouts' reports and orders were not inspected.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier General Kilpatrick (US), and Major General Wheeler and Lieutenant General Hampton (CS); the live page lists 'Hugh Kilpatrick' and Wheeler and omits Hampton. Kilpatrick, heading his report as brevet major general, says Hampton led the center (Butler's) division in the charge and that he himself regained the cavalry camp on foot and led the counterattack; Mitchell's infantry brigade came up about 8 o'clock without needing to fire. Wheeler, signing as lieutenant general, says he took command of his own and Butler's cavalry for the charge and covered the withdrawal with Dibrell's brigade.
claims.rationale: Kilpatrick and Wheeler give different accounts of who led the Confederate charge; neither is adopted, and the frozen and signed ranks differ. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Inconclusive and the live result Indecisive. Kilpatrick says his men retook the camp and artillery and drove the Confederates in confusion from the ground; Wheeler says that, though finally compelled to withdraw, the attack was a decided success. NPS says the Federals regained their artillery and camps and the Confederates withdrew as Union reinforcements approached.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The two commanders' characterizations conflict and are both preserved.

claims.value: The frozen and live casualty fields read 269 (US 183; CS 86). Kilpatrick reports his loss as 4 officers killed and 7 wounded, 15 men killed and 61 severely and several slightly wounded, and 103 officers and men taken prisoner, and says the Confederates left upward of 80 killed in his camp with many wounded; he took 30 prisoners. Wheeler says he secured some 350 prisoners and names three wounded generals. Kilpatrick's casualty table covers his division's losses for the whole campaign since Savannah (604).
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Kilpatrick's 103 prisoners lost and Wheeler's 350 taken disagree; Kilpatrick's campaign table is not assigned to this record.

open_questions: Hampton's No. 303 reports (read; they contain no narrative of March 10), Wheeler's March dispatches, Butler's and Humes's accounts, the Jordan, Atkins and Spencer brigade reports and regimental reports (Nos. 213–230), Mitchell's report and the nominal casualty list remain deferred. Cox's history (Chapter XI, read, not selected) also narrates the action; it is not one of this record's three families.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Blair's, G. P. Harrison's, Kilpatrick's, Wheeler's, J. D. Cox's, Bragg's, Slocum's, Hardee's and J. E. Johnston's reports and dispatches, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XLVII, Part 1, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. The No. 3 return of Union casualties is a compiler's table from nominal lists, used as the one targeted follow-up for the casualty gap at Kinston, Averasborough and Bentonville. Cox's history The March to the Sea; Franklin and Nashville (1882) belongs to the same author family as his report. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
